topic: Openleetcode: Local LeetCode Runner with In-Repo Tests

competitors.name: therepanic/openleetcode (the subject)
key_points: Local LeetCode runner written in Haskell, built with Cabal; Unlicense; 170 stars, 6 forks, 11 open issues; created 2026-01-12, last push 2026-09-04; latest release v1.0.4 (2026-08-17).

Differentiator: the test suites are open and live in the repo. Author's stated motivation: closed platforms never publish the test cases; he explicitly rejected the 'submit through the LeetCode API' approach used by other tools.
Flow: solution file -> matching problem manifest -> tiny language-specific harness -> pluggable execution backend -> local judge. CLI is described as 'just the glue'.
1,410 manifest.yaml files under tests/ (19,703 files total in tests/); repo badge reads '1.4k' problems.
12 language runtimes: cpp, rust, python3, python2, ruby, java, csharp, kotlin, go, dart, swift, typescript.
Backend is Piston (engineer-man/piston) over Docker at http://localhost:2000; first start installs runtimes and takes a while.

TEST_FORMAT.md is the contract: YAML manifest with entry(params/call per language), judge (exact|ignore_order), limits (time_ms/memory_mb), oracle (python3 checker), seed, tests; supports stress-test generation via a DSL.

Non-code contributions are scaffolded: generate_prompt.py, spartan.py (OpenRouter LLM drafts manifests into generated_problems/), molotov.py (fills sol.{lang}). Author says treat output 'like a junior contributor with infinite patience'.

competitors.name: skygragon/leetcode-cli
key_points: ~3,873 stars, JavaScript, last push 2026-03-04; the dominant CLI in this niche.
Works by authenticating and submitting to LeetCode's own API/judge — no local test cases, so it needs network + an account and inherits LeetCode's rate limits.
Direct contrast to openleetcode's 'no API submission, tests live locally' stance.

competitors.name: kawre/leetcode.nvim
key_points: ~2,204 stars, Lua, last push 2026-04-28; Neovim plugin for browsing and solving problems inside the editor.
Same API-driven model as leetcode-cli; strong on browsing/editor UX, but again no open local judge.

competitors.name: j178/leetgo
key_points: ~707 stars, Go, last push 2026-09-24 — the most actively maintained comparison point.
'Best LeetCode friend for geek': generates problem files, runs local tests from the statement's example cases, and can still submit to the platform.
Closest feature overlap, but its local testing is built from the examples in the statement, not from a maintained open test corpus.

competitors.name: judge0/judge0 + engineer-man/piston
key_points: judge0 ~4,459 stars (last push 2026-09-30) and piston ~2,824 stars (2026-07-31) are the sandboxed code-execution engines used to run untrusted submissions.
openleetcode uses Piston as its default backend, so its sandboxing story is inherited, not homegrown — relevant for the 'is it safe to run locally' question.

stats.fact: LeetCode hosts 4,069 problems total as of 2026-10-01 (3,284 free, 785 paid-only); difficulty split: 968 easy, 2,122 medium, 979 hard.
openleetcode ships 1,410 manifest files — about 34.6% of all LeetCode problems and ~43% of the free-tier problem set.
Repo has 170 stars, 6 forks, 11 open issues, 1 release cadence reaching v1.0.4 on 2026-08-17; written in Haskell with Cabal and released under the Unlicense.
12 language runtimes are supported, and the runtime templates intentionally mirror the official LeetCode environments so solutions look like normal submissions.
The Show HN launch (2026-08-18) reached 73 points and 19 comments — modest but real traction; the same project was posted to HN seven separate times between 2026-06-30 and 2026-08-18.
Default execution backend is Piston at localhost:2000, run via Docker Compose; Docker is a hard install requirement on Linux/macOS.

angles: The real story is the open test corpus, not the CLI: other tools re-submit to LeetCode's judge, openleetcode is the first to publish the tests themselves as a versioned, forkable artifact.
Coverage math: 1.4k problems is ~35% of LeetCode's 4,069 — concrete, checkable framing instead of 'lots of problems'.

The sync/staleness question the HN crowd raised: statements rarely change, but edge cases get patched; the project maintains its own tests plus a stress-test DSL, which is both the strength and the maintenance burden.
Trust problem of LLM-drafted manifests: the project itself warns that generated manifests are 'very much in need of review' — so the corpus quality is uneven by design.
It's Haskell, and that's load-bearing: contributors to the CLI need a Cabal toolchain, but non-code contributors only need to write YAML.
Practical setup reality check: Docker + Piston is a prerequisite, and the first backend start installs language runtimes and is slow — set expectations.
Known holes: no Concurrency, Shell, SQL, Design, or In-Place problem support yet, and premium problems are explicitly out of scope for now.
